name: German Bewegungskrieg and Auftragstaktik (1939-1941)

weightNotes.aggression: Offensive, short-war doctrine: Poland, Norway, France, Balkans and USSR were all opened by German attacks; the 1945 War Department handbook calls German leadership 'aggressive and daring' (TM-E 30-451 ch. IV).
weightNotes.maneuver: Kesselschlacht: panzer groups penetrated and closed pincers behind enemy armies (Minsk, Kiev, Vyazma 1941); House, Towards Combined Arms Warfare ch. 4 'The German Advance in Russia'.
weightNotes.flanking: Sichelschnitt 1940 put 7 of 10 panzer divisions through the Ardennes on a 70 km front against the weak hinge of the Allied line (House ch. 4; Frieser, Blitzkrieg Legend).
weightNotes.siegePreference: Targets were enemy field armies; cities were bypassed and left to the infantry (Warsaw, where 57 tanks were lost in one day, taught that tanks should avoid urban fighting; House ch. 4). Leningrad 1941 was invested rather than stormed.
weightNotes.reserveUse: Germany fought 1939-41 with almost everything forward and no real strategic reserve; panzer corps lacked the infantry to seal their own encirclements (House ch. 4). Low.
weightNotes.scouting: Armoured reconnaissance battalions and Luftwaffe air reconnaissance were good tactically (TM-E 30-451 ch. IV), but strategic intelligence badly underrated Soviet reserves and mobilisation capacity in 1941.
weightNotes.retreatThreshold: Basis: share of starting strength lost (killed, wounded, captured, missing) at the moment of withdrawal or break, never the battle total with pursuit. derived:breakpoint-quartile: modelRules.breakpoint.loserCasualtyShareAtBreak.worldwars mid 0.152, grade C. High cohesion and Kampfgruppe improvisation belong in snapshot cohesion; no source gives a doctrine-specific share at withdrawal (previous 0.3 was a judgment). Era baseline.
weightNotes.combinedArms: Panzer divisions habitually task-organised tanks, motorised infantry, artillery, engineers and flak into battlegroups (House ch. 4); Luftwaffe close support at Sedan 1940. Not 1.0 because air-ground coordination was poor in Poland and most infantry divisions stayed horse-drawn.
weightNotes.initiative: Auftragstaktik: orders gave the intent and left the method to subordinates; 'German tactical doctrines stress the responsibility and the initiative of subordinates' (TM-E 30-451 ch. IV). Commanders led from the front (Guderian, Rommel).
weightNotes.logisticsDiscipline: The army was geared to short distances, tied to railheads and horse transport with repairs sent back to Germany; panzer spearheads outran supply and maintenance in Russia 1941 (House ch. 4). Operations routinely exceeded supply.

summary: Germany concentrated its few panzer and motorised divisions into large masses at a decisive point, broke through with infantry, engineers, artillery and dive bombers, then drove the mobile divisions deep into the enemy rear to cut communications and encircle whole armies while the foot infantry followed to reduce the pockets. The Luftwaffe first won air superiority, then interdicted and supported the spearheads. Command was decentralised: commanders received an intent and acted on their own judgment, led from the front, and used radio in every tank to react faster than opponents could. 'Blitzkrieg' was not a formal doctrine; it was traditional Prussian Bewegungskrieg (war of movement) given engines and radios.
whyItWorked: Opponents deployed in linear cordons without depth or mobile reserves and commanded at First World War speed, so deep penetrations paralysed them psychologically and organisationally (House ch. 4). Poland fell in about five weeks, France and the Low Countries in six, and the 1941 encirclements destroyed most of the pre-war Red Army. Concentration, not superior tank numbers, was decisive: the Allies had more and often better tanks in 1940.
whereItFailed: The system assumed short campaigns. In Russia 1941 distances, mud and worn-out vehicles broke the logistics; encirclements leaked because panzer corps could not seal them; Soviet reserves were far larger than estimated, and the offensive stalled before Moscow in December 1941 and was thrown back by the Soviet counteroffensive. Against an enemy with depth and antitank strength the method stopped working (Kursk 1943). It could not cross the Channel (Battle of Britain 1940), and in North Africa supply across the Mediterranean, not tactics, set the limit.
